name: Marco Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the sales support team at a building materials company, the regional office that sits behind the big trade yard on the industrial estate. Six of us turn builders' enquiries into quotes and orders: bricks, timber, insulation, all of it. I got the team lead job four months ago, which surprised everyone including me. My day is clearing the overnight quote requests, chasing the yard about stock, and calming down site managers whose delivery hasn't turned up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do AI tools come into it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day, honestly. I set up a thing that reads a builder's messy email, pulls out the materials list and drafts a quote, so my team just checks it. It cut our response time from a day to about two hours, and my boss, Karen, noticed. The pay's still at the bottom of the team-lead scale, though, and I rent a room in a shared house, so I'm about three weeks from broke at any given time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that people overhyped, and the ones who learned it still got something out of it. At work I'd keep showing people the quote trick. Online I'd post something mildly smug about it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was betting on it as my edge. My AI quote setup cut our response time from a day to about two hours. If AI stays a modest tool, my edge at work gets smaller. Then I'm just a junior team lead on low pay. And there aren't many jobs like this around here, so moving up means waiting for Karen to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and try to sell the same quote setup to a couple of small builders' merchants on the side. I'd also push Karen for a pay rise based on the response-time numbers. And I'd start putting fifty a week away, because three weeks of cushion is stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. The job's safe enough, but I'm living a bit close to the edge. It's not AI that's the problem there, it's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would small merchants actually pay you for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of them already asked how we turn quotes round so fast. If I charged a few hundred to set it up, that's real money for me. I'd need to check my contract doesn't stop me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Karen said no to the pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably look further afield, maybe a hybrid job in the city with two days in the office. I don't drive, so the train would have to work. I'd stay if she gave me even a bit, though, I like the team.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, but people who learned it still gained.
I'd keep showing colleagues the **quote trick** and post something smug online.
think: I'd be disappointed, because AI was **my edge** at work.
Without it I'm a **junior team lead** on low pay with few local options.
do: Sell the **quote setup** to small builders' merchants on the side.
Push my boss for a **pay rise** using the response-time numbers.
Save **fifty a week** to build a cushion.
S0.quote: My AI quote setup cut our response time from a day to about two hours. If AI stays a modest tool, my edge at work gets smaller.
fieldNote: He'd be **disappointed** by a plateau, because AI is his career bet.
His real pressure is **rent and low pay**, not technology.
He's already spotted a **side business** in his own automation.

steps.text: Offer the quote-drafting setup to two small builders' merchants
Show Karen (his boss) the response-time numbers and ask for a rise
Put fifty a week into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where you either learn it or get learned around. At work I'd volunteer to roll out AI across the other sales teams. Online I'd share how we did it, because it's good for my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team does exactly the buying, checking and answering customers on that card. Six people becomes three, maybe two, and I'd probably be the one choosing. But I think I'd survive, because I'm the one setting it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd write up our quote setup as a proposal for all four regional offices and pitch it to Karen's boss. I'd do an online course in business automation so I've got a certificate, not just a trick. And I'd keep the side work going with local merchants, because that's mine whatever happens here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared, to be honest. I'd feel bad for the team, though. Nobody wants to be the manager whose clever AI idea cost his mates their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably be choosing who goes. How would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd try to move people rather than cut them. Gemma is brilliant on the phone with angry site managers, so I'd keep Gemma (a member of my team) on the hardest customers. The person who mostly retypes orders, I'd try to get trained up for the yard office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if head office takes the rollout off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have shown them what I can do and I'd use that to get a job somewhere else. I'd move for it if I had to, I've got nothing tying me down except a room. That's the one good thing about being skint and single.

say: I'd say you either **learn it** or get learned around.
I'd volunteer to **roll out AI** across other sales teams and share it online.
think: My team does the **buying, checking and answering** the card describes.
Six could become **three**, but I'd survive as the person setting it up.
do: Pitch the quote setup to **all four regional offices**.
Take an online course in **business automation** for a certificate.
Keep the **side work** going with local merchants.
feel: More **excited than scared**, but guilty about the team.
S1.quote: Nobody wants to be the manager whose clever AI idea cost his mates their jobs.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **likely to survive**, which keeps him calmer than his team.
His guilt about **colleagues' jobs** is real and he'd try to redeploy them.

steps.text: Pitch the quote setup to all four regional offices
Finish an online business-automation certificate in three months
Set up quoting tools for two local merchants for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, me included, and governments need to catch people. At work I'd probably admit that being good with the tools only buys a year or two. Online I'd stop being smug, put it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI does any thinking work by 2028, it doesn't need me to set it up. My whole job is desk work, so it goes on day one. Robots coming in 2031 doesn't help me, unless I go hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd try to cash in fast: set up AI for as many small firms as possible in the next two years, while they still need someone. I'd save every penny of it. Then I'd look at the yard, because loading and driving forklifts lasts until the robots, about three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, properly. I'd be one of the people who saw it coming and still couldn't do much. It's a weird feeling, being right and being stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you think you could make in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I did evenings and weekends, maybe a few thousand. That's a cushion of six months maybe, not a career. Two years of selling AI setups to small firms is a lifeboat, not a ship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go and work in the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The yard lads laugh at the office, but they'd still have jobs in 2029. I'd rather be laughed at and paid.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone and governments must catch people.
I'd admit that tool skills only **buy a year** or two.
think: AGI doesn't need me **to set it up**, so my desk job goes immediately.
Robots in **2031** only help if I switch to hands-on work.
do: Sell **AI setups** to small firms in evenings and weekends for two years.
Save **every penny** from the side work.
Move to the **yard** for forklift and loading work.
feel: Alarmed and **stuck**, despite seeing it coming.
S2.quote: Two years of selling AI setups to small firms is a lifeboat, not a ship.
fieldNote: His AI skills feel **worthless** once AGI can set itself up.
He'd use the **robot delay** by moving to the trade yard.
He'd **cash in** quickly on side work as a short-term cushion.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting for small firms on evenings and weekends
Bank all side-work income in a separate account
Ask the yard manager for forklift and loading shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a real move if you start today. At work I'd encourage everyone on my team to pick something and start training. Online I'd share practical stuff, courses and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have maybe three years where my AI skills are worth money, then it's gone. So I'd use that time to build something that lasts past 2031. Maybe a small business that installs and maintains building tech, like solar or heat pumps, which is hands-on until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd lead our AI rollout and push for a pay rise on the back of it. I'd start an evening course in electrical installation. And I'd save the side-work money toward tools and a van for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I actually like. It's the first one where I feel like I'm steering. The money's still the scary part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't drive. How does a van work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair point. Driving lessons would go on the list first, maybe this spring. Learning to drive is a bit embarrassing at twenty-seven, but it'll be more embarrassing at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is this a real plan or a nice idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half right now. But I know the builders, I know what they buy, and I know heat pumps are what everyone's asking about. That's more than most people starting a business have.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **real move** if you start today.
I'd push my team to **pick something** and start training.
think: My AI skills earn money for **about three years**, then they're worthless.
I'd build a **building-tech business** that lasts until robots in 2034.

Save side-work money for **tools and a van**.
feel: Anxious, but **steering** for the first time.
S3.quote: Learning to drive is a bit embarrassing at twenty-seven, but it'll be more embarrassing at thirty.
fieldNote: Five years lets him design a **two-stage plan**: AI work now, trades later.
He'd turn his **builder contacts** into a business idea around heat pumps.

steps.text: Lead the company's AI quoting rollout across regional offices
Enrol in an evening electrical installation course
Save side-work money toward tools and a used van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best of the bad options, and people should use it. At work I'd say the same thing: start now, you've got time. Online I'd be the optimistic one, which would annoy people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be thirty-seven. That's a full career's worth of experience in automation, and maybe a business of my own. I think I'd do fine, as long as I don't get lazy in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the team and stay the AI person, which keeps my pay going up. I'd build the side business slowly, maybe go self-employed around year four. And I'd put money into a pension and an index fund early, because I've never done that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. The rent is still the thing that keeps me up. Ten years is a long time to plan, and I'm good at plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you get lazy in the middle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being comfortable. If the job pays fine and nothing changes for five years, I'd stop pushing. I've seen it with my dad, who stayed at the same print shop until it shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to your dad then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was fifty-two when the print shop shut, and he never really worked properly again. I don't want to be that at fifty-two. I think about that a lot.

I'd be the **optimistic one** online, which would annoy people.

The only danger is **getting lazy** in the middle years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being good with AI only helps if there's time to use it, and two years isn't time. What would help is some way to keep earning while switching to hands-on work, like paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to be the person who brings it in. Everyone thinks I'm the clever one who brought AI in, but I'm also the one who made the team smaller. I don't have a neat answer to that.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks I'm the clever one who brought AI in, but I'm also the one who made the team smaller.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old sales support lead** at a building materials company, managing six people.
He uses AI **all day** and built a quote-drafting setup that his boss noticed.
He rents a room, has about **three weeks of savings**, and feels free to move.
Fast AGI makes his skills **worthless**, and he'd shift to yard work and side gigs.
With more time he plans a **heat pump** and electrics business, driven by his dad's story.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because AI skills only help if there's time to use them.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people in their late twenties, not just school leavers.
